en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.1 (SN 19.1, PTS SN ii 254) 1.
First Chapter: The Bone Discourse (Aṭṭhisutta)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Lakkhaṇa and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling on Mount Gijjhakūṭa.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached the Venerable Lakkhaṇa. Having approached him, he said to the Venerable Lakkhaṇa:
"Come, friend Lakkhaṇa, let us enter Rājagaha for alms.
"Very well, friend," the Venerable Lakkhaṇa replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
Then, as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, he manifested a smile at a certain spot.
Thereupon, the Venerable Lakkhaṇa said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"What, friend Moggallāna, is the cause, what is the reason for manifesting a smile?"
“Friend Lakkhaṇa, this is not the time for this question.
Ask this question of me in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Lakkhaṇa and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having walked for alms in Rājagaha, after their meal—
Having returned from their alms round, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the Venerable Lakkhaṇa said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
"Just now, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, while descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, you manifested a smile at a certain spot."
“Friend Moggallāna, what is the cause, what is the reason for your breaking into a sweat?
“Just now, friend, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a skeleton moving through the air.
Vultures, crows, and hawks were swooping down after it again and again, pecking at its interstices, tearing at it, and rending it.”
She then let out a cry of distress.
Then, friends, this occurred to me:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
“Such a being as this will come to be;
such a spirit (yakkha) as this will come to be;
such an acquisition of a personal existence (attabhāvapaṭilābha) as this will come to be.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, disciples indeed dwell as become of vision;
bhikkhus, disciples indeed dwell as become of knowledge, in that a disciple should know, see, or bear witness to such a thing as this."
"Monks, I had already seen that being before, yet I did not declare it.
If I were to declare this, others would not believe me;
and for those who do not believe me, that would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time."
"Monks, this being was once a butcher of oxen in this very city of Rājagaha.

Having been boiled in hell for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years as the ripening of that karma, through the remainder of the ripening of that same karma, he has come to such a state."
“...he experiences the acquisition of a personal existence.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 19.2 (SN 19.2, PTS SN ii 256) 1. First Chapter: The Lump of Flesh Sutta (Pesisutta) “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a lump of flesh, the size of a fig, fastened by a string, hanging from the neck of a man. It would not be easy to know whether it was near or far away. Why is that? Because of its smallness. So too, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, it is not easy to know where he will be reborn: in the company of the devas of the heaven of the Four Great Kings, or the devas of the Thirty-three, or the Yāma devas, or the Tusita devas, or the devas who delight in creation, or the devas who control the creations of others, or the devas of Brahmā’s retinue, or the devas of the retinue of Mahābrahmā. Why is that? Because of his smallness.”
“Here, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a piece of meat moving through the air.
Hawks, crows, and vultures were swooping down after it again and again, tearing at it and rending it.
It let out cries of distress... [as before]... ”
“Monks, this being was once a butcher of oxen right here in Rājagaha... [as before] ...

Saṃyutta Nikāya 19.5 (SN 19.5, PTS SN ii 257) 1. First Chapter: Hair-Splitting (Paṭhamavagga) The Discourse on Hair Like Sword Blades (Asilomasutta) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? “The person who is like a hair-splitter; the person who is like a sword-blade; the person who is like a razor; the person who is like a sharp-pointed blade; and the person who is like a butcher’s knife. “And how, monks, is one a person like a hair-splitter? Here, monks, a certain person, having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or his disciple, gains faith. Having gained faith, he goes to a forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects thus: ‘This Dhamma that has been well-expounded by the Blessed One is peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, and to be experienced by the wise, each for themselves. But this Dhamma is difficult to penetrate for me while I am still living the household life, crowded with children and wife, accustomed to Jātaka-maṃsa (meat), enjoying the use of sandalwood from Kāsi, wearing garlands, perfumes, and ointments, accepting gold and silver. It would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. “Then, monks, that person shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells withdrawn in body, speech, and mind; he is secluded, delights in solitude, and finds pleasure in seclusion. He does not associate with householders or renunciants, nor does he frequent their company. He dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. “Just as a man who splits a hair with a sharp razor, so too, monks, that person, having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or his disciple, gains faith... [as above] ...and dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. This, monks, is called a person like a hair-splitter. “And how, monks, is one a person like a sword-blade? Here, monks, a certain person... [reflects as before] ...‘It would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard... Then, monks, that person shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells withdrawn in body, speech, and mind; he is secluded, delights in solitude, and finds pleasure in seclusion. He does not associate with householders or renunciants, nor does he frequent their company. He dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. “Just as a man who draws a sword-blade from its scabbard, so too, monks, that person, having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or his disciple, gains faith... [as above] ...and dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. This, monks, is called a person like a sword-blade.

“And how, monks, is one a person like a razor? Here, monks, a certain person... [reflects as before] ...‘It would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard... Then, monks, that person shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells withdrawn in body, speech, and mind; he is secluded, delights in solitude, and finds pleasure in seclusion. He does not associate with householders or renunciants, nor does he frequent their company. He dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. “Just as a man who takes a razor from its case, so too, monks, that person, having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or his disciple, gains faith... [as above] ...and dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. This, monks, is called a person like a razor. “And how, monks, is one a person like a sharp-pointed blade? Here, monks, a certain person... [reflects as before] ...‘It would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard... Then, monks, that person shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells withdrawn in body, speech, and mind; he is secluded, delights in solitude, and finds pleasure in seclusion. He does not associate with householders or renunciants, nor does he frequent their company. He dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. “Just as a man who takes a sharp-pointed blade from its sheath, so too, monks, that person, having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or his disciple, gains faith... [as above] ...and dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. This, monks, is called a person like a sharp-pointed blade. “And how, monks, is one a person like a butcher’s knife? Here, monks, a certain person... [reflects as before] ...‘It would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard... Then, monks, that person shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells withdrawn in body, speech, and mind; he is secluded, delights in solitude, and finds pleasure in seclusion. He does not associate with householders or renunciants, nor does he frequent their company. He dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. “Just as a man who takes a butcher’s knife from its sheath, so too, monks, that person, having heard the Dhamma from the Tathāgata or his disciple, gains faith... [as above] ...and dwells aloof, detached, and indifferent to worldly things. This, monks, is called a person like a butcher’s knife. “These, monks, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. (This concludes the fifth discourse in the first chapter of the *Sakka-saṃyutta*.)

Saṃyutta Nikāya 19.8 (SN 19.8, PTS SN ii 257) 1. First Chapter: The Chapter on the Discourse on Sūciloma **Sūcilomasutta – The Discourse on Sūciloma** At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Sūciloma approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Sūciloma: “Sūciloma, what is your view? How do you see this? “Venerable sir, I hold this view: ‘The self and the world are eternal; only this is true, anything else is wrong. “What do you think, Sūciloma? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [The same exchange is repeated for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “What do you think, Sūciloma? When one directly knows and fully understands form as it really is with correct wisdom—its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—in such a way, does one regard it as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [The same is repeated for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “Therefore, Sūciloma, whatever form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling... Whatever perception... Whatever volitional formations... Whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one abandons desire for form, abandons desire for feeling, abandons desire for perception, abandons desire for volitional formations, and abandons desire for consciousness. With the abandoning of desire, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, the Venerable Sūciloma said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission! Then the Venerable Sūciloma received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the full admission. Not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Sūciloma, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. And the Venerable Sūciloma became one of the arahants.

1. First Chapter:
The Second Discourse on the Man with Hair Like Needles “Just now, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a man with hair like needles traveling through the air.”
Those needles entered his head and emerged from his mouth;
they entered his mouth and emerged from his chest;
they entered his chest and emerged from his belly.
Having entered through the belly, they emerge from the thighs;
having entered through the thighs, they emerge from the shanks;
having entered through the shanks, they emerge from the feet.
He then let out a cry of distress...
"Monks, this being was once a spy in this very city of Rājagaha...
...The ninth [sutta].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.10 (SN 19.10, PTS SN ii 258) 1. First Chapter: The Kumbhaṇḍa Discourse At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kumbhaṇḍas. What four? There is the kumbhaṇḍa who is ugly, deformed, and unsightly; there is the kumbhaṇḍa who is beautiful, handsome, and pleasing; there is the kumbhaṇḍa who is wealthy, possessing great wealth and property; and there is the kumbhaṇḍa who is poor, possessing little wealth and property. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of kumbhaṇḍas. Just as, bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kumbhaṇḍas, so too there are these four kinds of persons similar to kumbhaṇḍas in the world. What four? There is the person who is ugly, deformed, and unsightly; there is the person who is beautiful, handsome, and pleasing; there is the person who is wealthy, possessing great wealth and property; and there is the person who is poor, possessing little wealth and property. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons similar to kumbhaṇḍas in the world. [The Buddha then spoke in detail regarding each type: (1) “And how, bhikkhus, is a person ugly, deformed, and unsightly? Here, someone is ugly in form, with a repulsive appearance, and unsightly. This is called a person who is ugly, deformed, and unsightly. (2) And how is a person beautiful, handsome, and pleasing? Here, someone is beautiful in form, with a lovely appearance, and pleasing. This is called a person who is beautiful, handsome, and pleasing. (3) And how is a person wealthy, possessing great wealth and property? Here, someone has acquired wealth by right means, through effort, enterprise, and exertion, and that wealth is abundant. This is called a person who is wealthy, possessing great wealth and property. (4) And how is a person poor, possessing little wealth and property? Here, someone has not acquired wealth by right means, through effort, enterprise, and exertion, and that wealth is meager. This is called a person who is poor, possessing little wealth and property. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons similar to kumbhaṇḍas in the world. [The Buddha then gave a detailed exposition on the causes for each state. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition why some beings here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell? “Here, bhikkhu, some being destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. With the destruction of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and indulgence in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, he accumulates much demerit. On the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. This is the cause and condition why some beings here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. [The Buddha then explained the opposite case: “When, bhikkhu, a being does not destroy life, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence, he accumulates much merit.

On the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. This is the cause and condition why some beings here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. [The Buddha then explained the causes for ugliness and beauty: “And what, bhikkhu, is the cause and condition for a being to be ugly, deformed, and unsightly? Here, someone is full of anger and malevolence. This is the cause and condition for a being to be ugly, deformed, and unsightly. And what is the cause and condition for a being to be beautiful, handsome, and pleasing? Here, someone is free from anger and malevolence. This is the cause and condition for a being to be beautiful, handsome, and pleasing. And what is the cause and condition for a being to be wealthy, possessing great wealth and property? Here, someone is generous, open-handed, one who delights in charity, who gives appropriately, who enjoys relinquishing, and who is devoted to giving and sharing. This is the cause and condition for a being to be wealthy, possessing great wealth and property. And what is the cause and condition for a being to be poor, possessing little wealth and property? Here, someone is stingy, closed-fisted, one who does not delight in charity, who does not give appropriately, who does not enjoy relinquishing, and who is not devoted to giving and sharing. This is the cause and condition for a being to be poor, possessing little wealth and property. [The Buddha then spoke further: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kumbhaṇḍas. What four? There is the kumbhaṇḍa who is ugly, deformed, and unsightly; there is the kumbhaṇḍa who is beautiful, handsome, and pleasing; there is the kumbhaṇḍa who is wealthy, possessing great wealth and property; and there is the kumbhaṇḍa who is poor, possessing little wealth and property. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of kumbhaṇḍas. Just as, bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kumbhaṇḍas, so too there are these four kinds of persons similar to kumbhaṇḍas in the world. What four? There is the person who is ugly, deformed, and unsightly; there is the person who is beautiful, handsome, and pleasing; there is the person who is wealthy, possessing great wealth and property; and there is the person who is poor, possessing little wealth and property. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons similar to kumbhaṇḍas in the world. [The Buddha then gave a detailed exposition on the causes for each state. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu asked the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, what is the cause and condition why some beings here, upon the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell? “Here, bhikkhu, some being destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. “Just now, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a kumbhaṇḍa man traveling through the air.
As he went, he carried those very eggs on his shoulder;
when he sat down, he sat upon those very eggs.”
Vultures, crows, and hawks, swooping down one after another, tore at him and pecked at him.
He let out cries of distress...
[as before] ...Monks, this being was formerly a village headman in this very city of Rājagaha... [as before].
The tenth.
The first chapter.
Its summary (uddāna):
A bone, a piece of flesh, two ox-slaughterers,
a lump [of meat], a fowler, a ruthless butcher of sheep,
a sword, a pork-butcher, a spearman, and a cowherd.
Use the needle as a tool, O charioteer;
for he who sews is indeed a needle-bearer—
he was a village official carrying eggs.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.11 (SN 19.11, PTS SN ii 259) 2. Second Chapter: With Heads (Dutiyavagga) Sasīsakasutta: With Heads “Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a headless trunk; the person who is like a stump; the person who is like a leaning wall; and the person who is like a pillar. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one ‘like a headless trunk’? Here, bhikkhus, a person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, harbors ill will, and holds wrong view. This is called a person who is ‘like a headless trunk. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one ‘like a stump’? Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsehood, does not speak divisively, does not speak harshly, does not indulge in idle chatter, is not covetous, does not harbor ill will, and holds right view. Yet he is devoid of faith, shameless, and unafraid of wrongdoing. This is called a person who is ‘like a stump. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one ‘like a leaning wall’? Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life... [as above] ...and holds right view. He possesses faith, has a sense of shame, and is afraid of wrongdoing. Yet he is miserly regarding dwellings, miserly regarding families, miserly regarding gains, miserly regarding fame, and miserly regarding praise. This is called a person who is ‘like a leaning wall. And how, bhikkhus, is a person one ‘like a pillar’? Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life... [as above] ...and holds right view. He possesses faith, has a sense of shame, and is afraid of wrongdoing. He is not miserly regarding dwellings, not miserly regarding families, not miserly regarding gains, not miserly regarding fame, and not miserly regarding praise. This is called a person who is ‘like a pillar. These, bhikkhus, are the four persons found existing in the world.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time I was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove.
"In this case, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a man submerged up to his head in a cesspit... [and so on].

2. The Second Chapter:
The Discourse on the Dung-Eater “Here, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a man submerged in a cesspit, eating dung with both hands... [as above] ...”
“Monks, this being was none other than that wicked brahmin in this very city of Rājagaha.
Having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to a meal in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, he filled two wooden tubs with excrement and said:
‘Oh, sirs! Eat as much as you like and take it away! … [as before] …”
The Second.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.13 (SN 19.13, PTS SN ii 259) 2.
The Second Chapter.
The Discourse on the Flayed Woman:
“In this case, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a flayed woman traveling through the air.
Vultures, crows, and hawks were swooping down upon her again and again, tearing at her and rending her.”
She, indeed, raised a cry of distress...
"Monks, this woman was an adulteress right here in Rājagaha...

Second Chapter: The Section on Women Maṅgulitthi Sutta: The Ugly Woman At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a woman—ugly, unsightly, and misshapen; with a complexion like that of a withered leaf, with protruding veins, with a body covered in moles; hunchbacked, lame, and crippled; blind in one eye, afflicted by leprosy, rheumatism, or epilepsy; bald-headed, or with matted hair, or with disheveled hair; or else she might be a slave, dependent on others for her livelihood. She would go to a man who was handsome, attractive, graceful, wealthy, and of noble birth. Then that man would say to her: ‘Come, lady, let us enjoy ourselves together. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that woman consent to that? “Venerable sir, how could she not? That woman would certainly consent. “That is so, bhikkhus. For what reason? Because that woman is ugly, unsightly, and misshapen; because she has a complexion like that of a wither­ed leaf, with protruding veins, with a body covered in moles; because she is hunchbacked, lame, and crippled; because she is blind in one eye, afflicted by leprosy, rheumatism, or epilepsy; because she is bald-headed, or with matted hair, or with disheveled hair; or because she is a slave, dependent on others for her livelihood. “So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhunī may be ugly, unsightly, and misshapen; she may have a complexion like that of a withered leaf, with protruding veins, with a body covered in moles; she may be hunchbacked, lame, and crippled; she may be blind in one eye, afflicted by leprosy, rheumatism, or epilepsy; she may be bald-headed, or with matted hair, or with disheveled hair; she may be a slave, dependent on others for her livelihood. Yet she dwells restrained over the eye-faculty, guarded in the eye-faculty; she attains the destruction of the taints for which she has made the breakthrough. “Suppose, bhikkhus, that a man comes along carrying a load of sandalwood from the Himalayas. He would sell it to a merchant. The merchant, having bought it, would cut it into pieces and put them into a kiln to dry. Having dried them, he would split them into slivers and soak them in fragrant oil. Having soaked them, he would burn them and filter the oil. Then a man would come along who desired beauty, desired a good complexion, desired charm. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that man apply that oil to his head, his ears, or his nose? “Yes, venerable sir. “Would he anoint his body with it? “Yes, venerable sir. “Why is that? Because that oil is refined, highly refined, and of great value. “So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhunī may be ugly, unsightly, and misshapen... yet she dwells restrained over the eye-faculty, guarded in the eye-faculty; she attains the destruction of the taints for which she has made the breakthrough. “This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhunī who is ugly but beautiful within. 2. The Second Chapter:

The Discourse on the Woman Covered in Excrement “Just now, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a woman who was cooked, covered in excrement, and smeared with filth, traveling through the air.
She, indeed, cried out in distress...
[as before] ...Monks, this woman was formerly the chief queen of King Kaliṅga.
Driven by jealousy, she poured a basin of burning coals over her co-wife... [as before] ...
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.16 (SN 19.16, PTS SN ii 260) 2.
The Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga)
The Discourse on the Headless Trunk:
“Here, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a headless trunk moving through the air.
On its chest there were both eyes and a mouth.”
Vultures, crows, and hawks swooped down upon him again and again, tearing at him and rending him.
He let out cries of distress...
[as before] ...Monks, this being was none other than the executioner named Hārika in this very city of Rājagaha... [as before].
Sixth. Saṃyutta Nikāya 19.17 (SN 19.17, PTS SN ii 260) 2.
Second Chapter.
The Discourse on Evil Bhikkhus:
“Here, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a bhikkhu traveling through the air.
His outer robe was burning, blazing, and flaming; his bowl, too, was burning, blazing, and flaming.”
The waistband was burning, blazing, and glowing; his body too was burning, blazing, and glowing.
He indeed uttered cries of distress...
[as before] ...Monks, this monk was a wicked bhikkhu in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa... [as before].
Seventh.

The Discourse on the Trainee in Evil “I saw a trainee (sikkhamānā) traveling through the air.”

Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.20 (SN 19.20, PTS SN ii 262) 2. Second Chapter: The Discourse on the Wicked Novice At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a crow; the person who is like a monkey; the person who is like a butcher’s dog; and the person who is like a royal elephant. “And how, monks, is a person like a crow? Here, monks, some person, when criticized, becomes angry and bitter. When praised, he exults and becomes intoxicated. This, monks, is called a person who is like a crow. “And how, monks, is a person like a monkey? Here, monks, some person is fickle and unsteady in his behavior. This, monks, is called a person who is like a monkey. “And how, monks, is a person like a butcher’s dog? Here, monks, some person is greedy for gain, greedy for honor, and greedy for fame. This, monks, is called a person who is like a butcher’s dog. “And how, monks, is a person like a royal elephant? Here, monks, some person, when criticized, does not become angry or bitter; when praised, he does not exult or become intoxicated. He reflects thus: ‘If this person criticizes me, it must be because he sees some fault in me; if he praises me, it must be because he sees some virtue in me. Thus, monks, a noble disciple reflects upon both blame and praise. This, monks, is called a person who is like a royal elephant. “Monks, of these four kinds of persons, the one who is like a royal elephant is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent.”
“I saw a novice monk traveling through the air.
His outer robe was on fire...
[as before] ...he was an evil novice monk... [as before] ...”
The Tenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 19.21 (SN 19.21, PTS SN ii 262) 2.
The Second Chapter.
The Discourse on the Evil Novice Nun:
“Here, friends, as I was descending from Vulture Peak Mountain, I saw a novice nun traveling through the air.
Her outer robe was burning, blazing, and aflame; her bowl, too, was burning, blazing, and aflame.”
The waistband was burning, blazing, and glowing; my body too was burning, blazing, and glowing.
She, it is said, uttered a cry of distress.
Then, friends, this thought occurred to me:
‘It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir! There will be such a being;
there will be such a yakkha!’
“Such indeed will be the acquisition of a personal existence!
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, disciples truly dwell as those who have become eyes.”
"Monks, disciples indeed dwell as embodiments of knowledge, in that a disciple would know, see, or bear witness to such a thing.
Monks, I had already seen that novice girl before;
nevertheless, I did not declare it."
If I were to declare this, others would not believe me;
and for those who do not believe me, that would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
This, monks, was the evil novice nun in the dispensation of Kassapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Having been cooked in hell for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, and many hundreds of thousands of years as the result of that karma,
she now experiences such an acquisition of an individual existence due to the remaining residue of the ripening of that very same karma."
Eleventh. Second Chapter. Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
For that adulterer was submerged in a well;
that wicked brahmin became a dung-eater;
and that unfaithful woman became a skinless hag.
There was a woman of ill omen, a woman who practiced divination;
she was a defiler who scattered charcoal from funeral pyres,
and there was an executioner who severed heads.
A bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā,
a sāmaṇera, and also a sāmaṇerikā—
these are the going-forth in the Vinaya of Kassapa.
“They have committed evil deeds for so long.
The *Lakkhaṇa-saṃyutta* is completed.
